post.title: What a frost in May actually costs

body.p: On the night of May 19 it dropped to 29°F for about three hours. By morning, roughly a third of the tomato starts we'd set out the week before were black at the tips.

People ask what a frost like that costs, and the honest answer is: more than the plants. It's the plants, plus the two weeks we lost, plus the early-season prices we missed at market, plus the time spent replanting instead of weeding everything else.
We lost 212 starts. At what it costs us to grow them, that's a few hundred dollars of seed, soil and greenhouse heat. Annoying, but not the real number.
Our first tomatoes usually reach market the second week of July, when they sell for nearly double what they fetch in August. This year they arrived on July 28. That gap is where the money went.
Next spring we're trying row cover on every bed, every night, until June. It's tedious. It's also cheaper than another May like this one.
